hero.eyebrow: Musical dyslexia · not officially diagnosed, but real
hero.subheading: The notes are right there on the page. So why won't they hold still?
hero.dek: Dysmusia is a persistent difficulty reading, learning, or recognizing music — present since childhood, unrelated to effort or intelligence. It isn't an official diagnosis yet, but it's a real, recognizable pattern with a name and a growing body of research behind it.
hero.calloutText: Struggling to read music does not mean struggling to understand or make it. Some of the most accomplished musicians in history have worked almost entirely by ear.

ways.heading: Four ways in, when reading alone doesn't work
ways.intro: Multisensory instruction is well established for language-based dyslexia. The same logic applies to music: route the same information through more than one sense at once.

items.title: Visual
items.body: Color-coded notes and staff positions turn an abstract symbol into a pattern the eye catches quickly.

items.title: Auditory
items.body: Listening to a phrase before reading it gives the ear a target to match the page against.

items.title: Kinesthetic
items.body: Walking a floor staff, hand-signing pitch, or tracing notation adds movement and touch to the memory.

items.title: Imagination
items.body: A short mnemonic or character gives working memory something more durable than an abstract mark.

research.heading: The research is real, but still thin.
research.body: There isn't yet a large body of research specifically on music-reading difficulty, especially compared to dyslexia. What exists — from congenital amusia research to specialist case studies — suggests a real relationship worth taking seriously, alongside promising evidence that multisensory teaching helps.

hero.heading: Multisensory Learning
hero.dek: When reading notation in isolation doesn't work, routing the same information through other senses often does.

multisensoryLearning.intro: Multisensory instruction is well established for language-based dyslexia — approaches like Orton-Gillingham are built entirely around it. The same logic applies to music: instead of relying on sight-reading alone, these approaches route the same musical information through color, movement, sound, story, and touch, giving the brain more than one path to the same meaning.

senses.label: Color
senses.body: Assigning a consistent color to each note name or string turns an abstract symbol into a visual pattern the eye can catch quickly.
items: Color-coded strings or keys matched to color-coded noteheads
A "Colour Staff" system, where lines and spaces are tinted rather than plain black
Highlighting repeating visual landmarks (the same measure, the same interval shape) in a consistent color

senses.label: Movement
senses.body: Mapping pitch or rhythm onto the body or a physical space turns an abstract relationship into something felt.
items: A floor staff large enough to walk on, stepping "up" and "down" as pitch rises and falls
Conducting or clapping patterns that mirror note duration before ever reading it
Hand-signing pitch height (a system borrowed from Kodály-style teaching) alongside the printed note

senses.label: Sound
senses.body: Hearing a passage before reading it gives the ear a target to match the page against, instead of decoding cold.
items: Listening to a short phrase on repeat before attempting to read it
Singing a line by ear, then locating it on the staff afterward
Call-and-response rhythm games that build a felt sense of timing before notation is introduced

senses.label: Story
senses.body: Attaching a short story or image to a musical pattern gives working memory something more durable to hold onto than an abstract symbol.
items: Mnemonic phrases for line and space note names
Character-based stories for recurring rhythmic patterns ("the running notes," "the resting note")
Verbal patterns or chants that mirror a rhythm's shape

senses.label: Touch
senses.body: Physically manipulating notation — rather than only looking at it — adds a motor memory trace to a visual one.
items: Tracing notation with a finger while naming it aloud
Building phrases from movable, tactile note cards before writing them
Finger-position landmarks on an instrument tied to specific staff positions

hero.heading: A History of Music-Reading Difficulties
hero.dek: Not just the history of a word — the longer story of how researchers came to notice this pattern at all.

timeline.title: Early multisensory notation teaching
timeline.body: Margaret Hubicki develops the Colour Staff system for teaching notation, years before multisensory literacy instruction became widely recognized in the UK.

timeline.title: Early prevalence estimates
timeline.body: Kalmus and Fry publish early estimates distinguishing self-reported "tone-deafness" from measured perceptual difficulty with music, laying groundwork for later prevalence research.

timeline.title: Congenital amusia research develops
timeline.body: Isabelle Peretz, Julie Ayotte, and colleagues at the University of Montreal study adults with lifelong musical-listening difficulty, establishing it as a distinct, measurable perceptual pattern rather than a vague self-description.

timeline.title: "Musical dyslexia" proposed
timeline.body: Retired pediatric neurologist Dr. Neil Gordon coins the term, explicitly drawing the parallel to dyslexia and dyscalculia.

timeline.title: Music-and-dyslexia specialists collect case studies
timeline.body: Music teachers and language therapists — including T. R. Miles and John Westcombe, editors of Music and Dyslexia — begin compiling case studies and early research specifically on notation-reading difficulty in dyslexic musicians.

timeline.title: Growing but still thin research base
timeline.body: Interest in the overlap between dyslexia and music grows among educators, but the research base remains small relative to language-based dyslexia — leaving most working knowledge in the hands of specialist teachers rather than large studies.
